COLORED ORPHANS ASYLUM.—The Twelfth Anniversary
of the Colored Orphans Asylum at the Tabernacle was attended
last
night by a large audience. The children went through
their exercises in reading, singing, geography, and other
branches in a manner highly creditable to themselves
and their teachers. Among them Henry, a Bushman
boy, brought to this country by Mr. Chase, took part in dialogue got up for the occasion,
and spoke the language with considerable fluency. Dr.
McCune Smith, Physician of the Institution, made
a short and very interesting address describing the work
in connection with which the following letter
from Mr. Chase to the Committee of the Lyceum of
Natural History of this City was produced:


I beg to state for his information of your Scientific
Society that the Bushman whom I have brought from South
Africa into my possession between four and five years
ago from the hands of traders who, according to our
knowledge, through the Bushman country, the traders upon
the Bushman during the time he traded his turn
from expedition, and had murdered of us
poor many dead bodies being constantly in view,
I found him in his state and remained with the boy Henry, picked
him up, placed him in his wagon, nursed him until he
quite recovered, and brought him to town. On the
occasion of his starting again for the Interior, the trader
requested me to take charge of him.


I have succeeded in teaching him to speak the English
language, but with great trouble have found it difficult
to command his attention. I have however taught him by
the sounds, so he could recollect them. Thus, he
now pronounces them pretty correctly. When errors were
made, the boy seemed to be in chains himself,

FRIENDS SOCIETY.—This Society of amateur
performers celebrated their Fifth Anniversary at the
Apollo on Wednesday evening. The performances
were preceded by remarks by the President, giving a short
history of the Association. A century since the originators together in
Hall in William st. organized themselves and have sung
since that period, given concerts to their
friends. The founders, but one remains whose grey
hairs are not yet whitened with the age, is Mr.
Winters. He still lives and will probably attend future
celebrations. The performances consisted of elevated
orchestral music interspersed by songs, from Ass. Kirk-
ham, etc. We believe, in New York, we
noticed few professionals in the orchestra, but we are
informed that they have rarely given concerts with
so little erroneous aid, and thus, their numbers are now
remarkably large. Miss Kirkham is a young English
girl of modest and unassuming appearance. She was
announced a pupil from the Conservatoire Royale de
Musique in Paris. She has a soft, musical voice,
carefully trained and would appear very well in
a parlor, but lacks force and expression. Her perform-
ances were well received by the company. The piano
accompaniment on one of Messrs. instruments, was
played by a Loder. The gem of the evening was a
trumpet solo by Hesse, of the former German Com-
pany. An anthem was also performed, which was last
played many years since by this Society, and was the
first symphony produced in New York by an orchestra,
and was kept up for an hour with great spirit.


STARTING EARLY.—On Monday afternoon Mr.
Comstock, Conductor of the New Haven train, noticed a
slightly little boy of about five years old in the car,
who seemed to be without anyone. Before the
train reached Greenwich, he ascertained that the child
was Edward Hyer, that he lived in Avery st. in
this City, and that his return from school having
taken a fancy ride in the cars, he had left without
any idea of where he was going. He was quite gen-
teelly dressed and seemed to enjoy his trip exceedingly. The New York Palladium of Tuesday gives the
rest of this misadventure follows:


It is impossible to send the boy home.
New York, this morning. Mr. Comstock took him in charge and
their staff here carried him to his lodgings the Town
House, where he was kindly cared for by Mr. Hubbs, the
clerk. Having been in for hours by the
duty of the establishment, he said
possibly he would have got into his cot at home.
After lying down, he repeated to his escort his
dropped sleep was aided by his journey, but as he
started on his novel position, this morning Mr. Com-
stock carried him discontinuously back to New York,
and doubtless returned him in safety to his friends.

noticed the arrest of Mr. W. A. Colt of No. 90 Al-

Ezekiel Willis (also of Brooklyn) to make an assignment
of his effects, the former with view of enabling
the latter to defraud his principal creditors, Messrs
Stannard & No. 210 Water st. and Mr. Jones of this
City. In Justice B. Mr. Colt could not
state that he appeared before Justice Osborne at the
time appointed in the case, but that the com-
plainant was not in attendance, and it subsequently
ascertained that he had precipitously left for California
aboard the brig Sarah Heffaud, before Mr. Colt was

and when I walked up this morning, and
found that I was well, thanked God for taking care of me."

half whisper. He paused after it—conscience was at its work.

"Should you?"

arm, and all over you, and cannot keep it
beating, nor can you—nobody can but God.

It will be seen that The Resolutions via Committee were adopted—after a week's deliberation on Saturday, by very decided majorities in both Houses; we presume the vote upon Mr. Thomas's resolution is the best test of the sentiment of the House. We are very well content with the Resolutions as they were; as Congress has, on divers occasions, undertaken to control the actions of the General Government by Resolutions. We would respectfully ask if there is man in the community who believes that, in any one instance these Resolutions ever had the remotest influence upon Congress. As a declaration of the views, it is an important subject; we, of course, can have no objection to the present, but we have not the strictest confidence in their efficacy.

It will be that Mr. Berrien's motion, lost by the Meeting of Southern members, has prevailed in the General Committee, and that an address is to be prepared to the whole Union and to the South. Mr. Berrien has been made the Chairman of the Sub-Committee in place of Mr. Calhoun. We predict the whole Affair will fizzle out; enough of diversity of sentiment has already been manifested to deprive whatever may be done of all moral or political influence.

A well-informed Washington Correspondent of the Philadelphia North American says that at the meeting of the General Committee, on Thursday last, Mr. Senator King was in the chair.

Mr. Berrien renewed his motion that an address be prepared for the Union and the South alone; it carried in the committee, consisting of Messrs. Berrien, Calhoun, Abel, and Abbis, newly appointed; it is thought the original address with amendments will be reported back and that majority and minority reports will be submitted.

Mr. Calhoun's address was carried in the Committee by one vote, by proxies; being Mr. Sebastian, whose proxy Mr. Foote said if he had been present he should have voted against the address, that it would have been lost; so says the Correspondent of the North Am.
